paragraphs: Iterative self-improvement trains a language model on its own outputs after a reward signal filters out unsuitable examples. This paper develops a theory for that process when each training round has only a finite number of samples. It represents each round as maximum-likelihood training on the filtered output distribution and derives guarantees for the model’s expected reward.

The analysis identifies a feedback loop: a better model produces more outputs that pass verification, providing more accepted training data for the next round. This helps explain how improvement can sustain itself across iterations. The same analysis also explains why improvement eventually saturates, rather than continuing indefinitely.

The authors then consider tasks at different difficulty levels. They prove conditions involving the starting model, task difficulty, and sample budget under which an easy-to-hard curriculum has better guarantees than a fixed task mixture. Simulations, synthetic graph reasoning, and mathematical reasoning experiments support the analysis. The curriculum advantage is conditional on those factors, rather than a claim that every model benefits from the same ordering.
icml-2026-a-task-centric-theory-for-iter.tldr: A finite-sample theory explains self-improvement feedback and identifies conditions under which easy-to-hard curricula offer better reward guarantees.

paragraphs: When a classifier combines several views of an example, it needs to decide how much evidence each view contributes. This paper identifies a scale mismatch in existing evidential fusion rules: large numerical prediction scores can be treated as strong semantic confidence. Consequently, a view with inflated but uninformative scores can dominate the combined prediction.

Scale-Invariant Evidential Fusion, or SAEF, standardizes scores separately for each instance to separate their scale from their confidence contribution. It then combines views through statistical consensus instead of allowing raw magnitude to determine influence. The central idea is that changing how large a view’s scores are should not, by itself, make that view more persuasive.

The authors theoretically establish invariance to global scaling and robustness to asymmetric dominance. Experiments on four datasets report better accuracy and robustness than leading baselines when views contain noise or conflicting semantic information, together with stability under severe scale changes. These findings connect a specific mathematical property of the fusion rule to the observed reliability of combined predictions.
icml-2026-beyond-magnitude-scale-invaria.tldr: SAEF standardizes evidence before combining views, preventing inflated score magnitudes from dominating classification.

paragraphs: A unified multimodal model can understand an instruction yet struggle to turn that understanding into an accurate image. This paper separates that gap into difficulties with planning complex requests and correcting visual imperfections through unstructured feedback. Its proposed framework teaches models to choose a generation strategy according to instruction complexity and their own capability.

The training pipeline provides three types of execution paths. Simple requests can use direct generation, outputs needing improvement can use self-reflection, and complex requests can use multiple planning steps. A hierarchical data pipeline supplies more than 50,000 examples, followed by supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

The reinforcement learning design rewards reasoning at individual steps for logical consistency and applies a complexity penalty within groups to discourage redundant computation. Together, these mechanisms aim to make extra reasoning useful without making it the default for every request. Experiments report better image-generation fidelity than existing baselines across simple and complex instructions. The contribution is an adaptive approach to generation and refinement within a unified model.
icml-2026-breaking-dual-bottlenecks-evol.tldr: An adaptive training framework teaches unified multimodal models when to generate directly, reflect, or plan across multiple steps.

paragraphs: Benchmark scores can be difficult to interpret in terms of work people actually perform. Human completion time offers a more familiar measure of difficulty, but collecting those timings is expensive and noisy. BRIDGE estimates a shared difficulty scale from model responses and connects that scale to human task duration.

The framework uses a two-parameter logistic Item Response Theory model to jointly estimate task difficulty and model capability across benchmarks. The authors find a linear relationship between this latent difficulty and the logarithm of human completion time. Once that relationship anchors the scale, model performance alone can be used to infer human completion times for new benchmarks.

BRIDGE also expresses frontier model capability as a human task-length horizon. The authors independently reproduce METR’s exponential scaling result, with the duration of tasks solvable at a 50% success level doubling approximately every six months. This is a finding about the inferred capability trend, not the time a model itself takes to execute a task. The framework makes benchmark performance more interpretable through a common human-time reference.
icml-2026-bridge-predicting-human-task-c.tldr: BRIDGE links model-derived task difficulty to human completion time, enabling capability comparisons in terms of human task length.

paragraphs: Statement autoformalization translates mathematical language into a formal representation. This paper argues that treating formal code simply as a sequence overlooks the nested logical structure of mathematical statements. Decompose, Structure, and Repair, or DSR, makes that structure explicit so translation and error correction can operate on meaningful components.

DSR first decomposes a statement into logical parts and organizes them into an operator tree. This tree supplies a structural blueprint for locating errors and refining the affected subtrees. Its modular design connects language-model generation with symbolic structure, allowing repairs to target particular logical components rather than treating the entire statement as an undifferentiated output.

The paper also introduces PRIME, a benchmark containing 156 undergraduate and graduate theorems from canonical textbooks, with expert annotations in Lean 4. Experiments report a new best result and consistent improvements over baselines under equivalent computational budgets. These findings support the usefulness of explicit hierarchy for autoformalization: representing how a statement’s parts fit together can improve both the translation process and its subsequent repair.
icml-2026-decompose-structure-and-repair.tldr: DSR organizes mathematical statements into operator trees to guide formal translation and targeted error repair.

paragraphs: Knowing that a final answer is uncertain does not reveal where a long reasoning process went wrong. Stepwise Confidence Attribution, or SCA, assigns confidence to individual reasoning steps using generated traces, without requiring access to a language model’s internal workings. It is designed to make failures in closed-source models easier to locate.

The framework uses the Information Bottleneck principle to identify useful agreement across correct solutions. Steps that match shared reasoning structures receive higher confidence, while departures are treated as possible errors. NIBS measures consistency without constructing graphs. GIBS instead learns relevant subgraphs through a differentiable mask, allowing the assessment to account for variation in logical structure.

Experiments on mathematical reasoning and multi-hop question answering find that low-confidence steps are strongly associated with reasoning errors. Using these step-level signals to guide self-correction improves correction success by up to 13.5% compared with answer-level feedback. The confidence scores therefore provide a practical diagnostic signal rather than a proof that a particular step is incorrect, and their finer resolution helps direct corrective effort.
icml-2026-diagnosing-multi-step-reasonin.tldr: SCA uses agreement across correct reasoning traces to flag uncertain steps and improve self-correction without internal model access.

paragraphs: Federated learning lets clients collaborate without exchanging their local data, but different client distributions can pull training in conflicting directions. FedCDWA addresses this heterogeneity through a framework that separates personalized distillation on clients from mutual distillation on the server. This separation is intended to reduce optimization conflicts introduced by the distillation process itself.

The framework combines class prototypes through Hierarchical Wasserstein Aggregation. This aggregation avoids restrictive parametric assumptions while seeking to retain both structure within each class and geometric relationships between classes. A second mechanism, Prototype–Variance Dual Alignment, aligns feature means and variances, so matching is sensitive to both the location and spread of feature distributions.

The authors prove convergence guarantees and evaluate the method on three datasets at different heterogeneity levels. They report consistent gains in both global and personalized accuracy, with smaller performance losses as client differences become more severe. The results suggest that separating the learning roles and preserving richer distributional structure can make collaborative learning more stable when clients do not share the same data distribution.
icml-2026-fedcdwa-decoupled-federated-pr.tldr: FedCDWA separates client and server distillation while aligning feature distributions to improve federated learning under heterogeneous data.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning systems may train using policies supplied by third parties. This paper examines how that dependency creates an opening for backdoor attacks. Earlier attacks commonly assumed access to a victim’s parameters, rewards, or observations; the proposed Supply-Chain Backdoor attack, or SCAB, demonstrates an attack route without those white-box privileges.

SCAB poisons training data through legitimate agent–environment interactions available through a black-box interface. The important shift is the point of influence: a third-party policy can affect the data used for learning even when the attacker cannot directly manipulate the victim’s internals. This makes the training supply chain part of the system’s security boundary.

The reported experiments use only 3% data corruption, reach a peak attack success rate above 90%, and reduce victim returns by 80%. The peak figure describes the strongest reported success rather than a universal success rate. Together, these results demonstrate that limited corruption entering through external agents can have substantial effects on learned behavior, highlighting the practical risk of treating third-party training interactions as inherently trustworthy.
icml-2026-fox-in-the-henhouse-supply-cha.tldr: SCAB demonstrates that third-party policies can introduce effective reinforcement learning backdoors through black-box training interactions.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why a transformer trained on synthetic planetary motion may fail to learn an internal Newtonian model. It studies how general inductive biases shape the physical explanation the model acquires. The authors identify spatial smoothness, spatial stability, and temporal locality as decisive ingredients in their planetary-motion setting.

Spatial smoothness keeps nearby physical positions meaningfully related in the representation. Naive tokenization can disrupt this relationship, so the authors formulate prediction as regression rather than classification. Spatial stability concerns resistance to noise; they teach it by having the model correct perturbations introduced into its context. These changes address how the model represents space and responds to imperfect observations.

With smoothness and stability established, imposing temporal locality induces a Newtonian representation based on gravitational forces. Without that additional bias, the model instead learns a Keplerian representation that fits elliptical parameters. The findings show that successful prediction can arise from different internal descriptions. They also suggest that relatively general structural guidance can steer learning toward a specific physical model without explicitly supplying the underlying law.
icml-2026-from-kepler-to-newton-inductiv.tldr: Experiments on planetary motion show how spatial and temporal inductive biases steer transformers toward Newtonian or Keplerian world models.

paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning increasingly combines rewards for different goals, such as correctness and following output constraints. This paper finds that applying Group Relative Policy Optimization directly in this setting can erase useful distinctions. Different combinations of rollout rewards can become identical advantage values, leaving training unable to distinguish outcomes that differ across objectives.

The proposed Group reward-Decoupled Normalization Policy Optimization, or GDPO, normalizes individual rewards separately. This preserves their relative differences more faithfully before they guide policy optimization. The motivation is that a training signal must retain information about the separate goals if the model is to improve across them. The authors connect the loss of that information in GRPO to poorer convergence and, in some cases, early training failure.

Tests cover tool calling, mathematical reasoning, and coding reasoning, assessing correctness alongside format and length constraints. GDPO consistently outperforms GRPO across the evaluated settings and substantially improves training stability. These results support reward-specific normalization as a useful change for multi-reward learning, with evidence spanning several distinct language-model tasks.
icml-2026-gdpo-group-reward-decoupled-no.tldr: GDPO normalizes rewards separately to preserve distinctions that standard GRPO can lose during multi-objective language-model training.

paragraphs: Video depth estimation must recover spatial detail while keeping its predictions coherent as the camera and scene change. This paper argues that temporal smoothing alone struggles to preserve three-dimensional consistency, especially during rotations or major viewpoint changes. GemDepth instead builds camera motion and scene geometry into the features used for depth prediction.

Its Geometry-Embedding Module estimates camera poses between frames and uses those estimates to generate implicit geometric embeddings. These motion cues guide an Alternating Spatio-Temporal Transformer toward correspondences between scene points across frames. Connecting observations through their geometric relationships is intended to retain sharp local details while making depth predictions agree over time.

GemDepth also uses a data-efficient training strategy to combine efficiency with geometric consistency. Evaluations across multiple datasets report state-of-the-art performance, with particular strength in complex dynamic scenes. The stated findings support the paper’s central design choice: temporal agreement becomes more useful when informed by how the camera moves and how observations relate in three dimensions, rather than being treated solely as similarity between successive frames.
icml-2026-gemdepth-geometry-embedded-fea.tldr: GemDepth uses camera-motion embeddings to guide video depth prediction toward sharper details and stronger three-dimensional consistency.

paragraphs: Cross-modal retrieval learns relationships between different kinds of data, but web-collected training pairs can contain incorrect matches. This paper argues that filtering examples or choosing a single replacement target leaves learning vulnerable to a bad individual choice. A discrete replacement also compresses potentially richer neighborhood information into one selected proxy.

Intra-modal Neighbor-aware Noise Rectification, or IN2R, constructs a soft supervision target from multiple related examples. A dynamic Cross-Model Memory supplies neighbors, and a Graph Refiner reasons over their relationships. The resulting continuous prototype represents agreement within a local semantic neighborhood, using structure inside each modality to help repair mismatches between modalities.

This approach makes neighborhood consensus the basis for correcting supervision rather than simply replacing one questionable match with another. Experiments on Flickr30K, MS-COCO, and CC152K report significant improvements over state-of-the-art methods. The findings support the usefulness of synthesizing a target from relational evidence when cross-modal pairings are noisy. The method’s rationale rests on the geometric stability available within modalities, which supplies the information used for that synthesis.
icml-2026-intra-modal-neighbors-never-li.tldr: IN2R repairs noisy cross-modal supervision by synthesizing soft targets from graph-based reasoning over neighboring examples.

paragraphs: Graph foundation models are intended to transfer across tasks whose relevant structures may span very different distances. Pretraining with a fixed number of graph hops imposes a fixed context size, which can mismatch those tasks. R-GFM addresses this problem by making structural scale an explicit part of the model’s representation.

The method samples subgraphs at different hop distances and connects them in a graph-of-graphs. It then learns representations using Riemannian geometry that adapt to the represented structure. This gives the model access to several scales rather than committing its pretraining context to one neighborhood size. That matters when the useful structural context of a downstream task is heterogeneous or unknown in advance.

The theoretical analysis shows reduced structural domain generalization error compared with fixed-scale graph foundation models. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance across various datasets, including up to 49% relative improvement on downstream tasks. That maximum is a reported gain, not an across-task average. Together, the analysis and experiments support explicitly modeling scale as a route toward more transferable graph representations.
icml-2026-learning-graph-foundation-mode.tldr: R-GFM models multiple graph scales through a Riemannian graph-of-graphs to improve transfer across structural contexts.

paragraphs: This paper studies a counterintuitive training effect: repeatedly using fewer examples can require less computation to learn than using a larger dataset. The authors observe this small-versus-large gap across algorithmic tasks, model architectures, and optimizers. Their question concerns the dynamics of learning, rather than simply how much distinct data is available.

They argue that sampling biases in smaller datasets can encourage appropriate growth across the model’s layers. Because these biases are more pronounced with fewer samples, repeated exposure can create a favorable direction for optimization. The paper develops a theoretical analysis and uses empirical interventions to support this proposed explanation for the training speedup.

The findings suggest that dataset repetition can be a deliberate optimization choice, particularly for reasoning tasks, instead of serving only as a response to scarce data. The claim is that smaller repeated datasets can help under the investigated conditions; it does not establish that reducing data always improves training. The broader contribution is an explanation of how the composition and reuse of training samples can influence learning speed.
icml-2026-less-data-faster-training-repe.tldr: The paper links faster learning from repeated smaller datasets to sampling biases that encourage favorable layer-wise growth.

paragraphs: A medical multimodal model can produce convincing language while misunderstanding the geometry of an image. This paper calls that deficit geometric blindness and connects it to training that prioritizes linguistic fluency over spatial fidelity. Med-Scout targets the perceptual problem through reinforcement learning based on geometric information already present in unlabeled medical images.

The framework obtains verifiable supervision from three proxy tasks: Hierarchical Scale Localization, Topological Jigsaw Reconstruction, and Anomaly Consistency Detection. These tasks are inspired by systematic clinical reading and reasoning. They provide a way to train geometric perception without relying on costly expert annotations, grounding the learning signal in image structure rather than only in the plausibility of generated text.

The authors introduce Med-Scout-Bench specifically to measure geometric perception. They report that Med-Scout outperforms leading proprietary and open-source models by over 40% on this benchmark and substantially reduces the identified deficit. Improvements also extend to radiological and broader medical visual question answering. These results indicate that strengthening geometric perception can benefit medical understanding beyond the proxy tasks used during training.
icml-2026-med-scout-curing-mllms-geometr.tldr: Med-Scout uses geometry-based reinforcement learning on unlabeled medical images to improve spatial perception and medical question answering.

paragraphs: Stochastic optimization chooses actions when costs depend on uncertain outcomes. With limited data, even the probability distributions governing those outcomes may be poorly known. This paper proposes choosing decisions by minimizing an upper confidence bound on expected cost, making uncertainty about the estimated cost part of the optimization objective.

The central statistical construct is the Average Percentile Upper Bound, or APUB. It serves as an upper bound for population means and as an approximate risk measure for sample means. The authors prove asymptotic correctness and consistency, providing theoretical support for its behavior as the amount of data grows. These are specifically asymptotic properties rather than an unrestricted claim about every finite dataset.

The paper develops a bootstrap approximation and an L-shaped solution method, focusing on two-stage linear stochastic problems with random recourse. Demonstrations on a two-stage product mix problem report benefits for reliability and consistency under uncertainty about the underlying distribution. The approach connects statistical uncertainty to the decision rule itself, seeking robust choices through a conservative estimate of expected cost.
icml-2026-minimizing-upper-confidence-bo.tldr: APUB optimization minimizes an upper confidence bound on expected cost to account for poorly known probability distributions.

paragraphs: Online conformal prediction aims to produce informative prediction intervals while maintaining a target long-run coverage rate, even for arbitrary or adversarial data streams. Existing methods often depend on learning-rate tuning. This paper develops a general theoretical connection between an online algorithm’s regret and the coverage of the intervals it produces.

The key quantity is linearized regret under the pinball loss. The authors show that controlling this quantity yields coverage bounds through a black-box reduction involving the Fenchel conjugate of a regret bound. This provides a reusable route from an online learning guarantee to a coverage guarantee, rather than requiring a separate coverage analysis for each algorithm.

Using that connection, they construct UP-OCP by reducing interval prediction to a two-asset portfolio selection problem and applying universal portfolio algorithms. The resulting method is parameter-free and has finite-time miscoverage bounds, including for polynomially growing predictions. Experiments report consistently better interval-size and coverage trade-offs than prior online conformal baselines. The contribution combines a general analytical tool with a concrete method that avoids manual learning-rate selection.
icml-2026-online-conformal-prediction-vi.tldr: UP-OCP uses universal portfolio algorithms and a regret-to-coverage theory to produce prediction intervals without learning-rate tuning.

paragraphs: In long-tailed recognition, rare classes have too little data to estimate reliable feature distributions. Reconstruction methods can borrow information or synthesize features, but their statistical changes may make similar classes harder to distinguish. Risk-Bounded Distribution Reconstruction, or RBDR, adds controls to these updates within a two-stage pipeline using frozen features.

RBDR adjusts both distribution means and covariances. For a proposed mean change, it uses a soft projection onto a supportive set so that an upper bound on surrogate discriminative risk does not increase. For covariance, it reduces spread along directions associated with rival classes while preserving diversity in orthogonal directions. This targets the geometry of class confusion instead of shrinking variation indiscriminately.

The risk control concerns a surrogate upper bound, so it should not be read as a guarantee that every actual classification error decreases. Experiments across multiple long-tailed benchmarks nevertheless report better performance and stability. The contribution is a way to turn heuristic reconstruction suggestions into controlled statistical updates, especially when scarce tail data makes those suggestions unreliable.
icml-2026-risk-bounded-distribution-reco.tldr: RBDR controls mean and covariance updates for rare classes to improve reconstruction stability and class separation.

paragraphs: Adversarial perturbations can disrupt the alignment between images and text in models such as CLIP. Many defenses require labeled adversarial fine-tuning, which limits their usefulness in zero-shot settings. This paper introduces Self-Calibrated Consistency, or SCC, a test-time defense motivated by weaknesses in attacks’ semantic guidance and their sensitivity to changes of view.

SCC combines semantic and spatial consistency. Its semantic module uses soft pseudo-labels from a counterattack warm-up and predictions across multiple views to stabilize image–text alignment and distinguish the target embedding from confusable alternatives. Its spatial module aligns visual predictions across augmented views, seeking agreement despite adversarial perturbations. Together, these modules form a plug-and-play inference strategy.

Experiments on 22 benchmarks and diverse attack settings report consistent improvements in CLIP’s zero-shot robustness while maintaining accuracy. The method also integrates with other vision-language models for further gains. These findings support using consistency at inference time as a defense mechanism, with broader relevance suggested for models such as BioMedCLIP. The reported gains concern the evaluated attacks and benchmarks.
icml-2026-self-calibrated-consistency-ca.tldr: SCC improves adversarial robustness at test time by enforcing semantic and spatial consistency across image views.

paragraphs: Solving time-dependent differential equations quickly often requires a compromise: small time steps improve trajectory fidelity but increase runtime, while large steps can distort the solution. Dynamical System Machines offer another computational route through continuous physical evolution. This paper develops DS-TS to help such machines represent the complex spatial and temporal interactions these equations require.

DS-TS introduces three mechanisms. Excitatory–inhibitory inspired coupling models complex spatial interactions. State-aware dynamic nonlinearity supports correlations that change with the system’s state. Hierarchical temporal integration captures higher-order dependencies over time. These components address different aspects of the same problem: representing a system whose behavior depends jointly on spatial relationships and temporal evolution.

Experiments report high-fidelity solutions alongside approximately a thousandfold speed improvement and a hundred-thousandfold energy-efficiency improvement relative to baseline solvers. These are reported experimental comparisons rather than universal speed guarantees. The results suggest that improving the representational capabilities of physical dynamical computation can make it useful for time-critical equation solving, where both accurate trajectories and low latency are central requirements.
icml-2026-solving-time-dependent-differe.tldr: DS-TS equips physical dynamical computation with spatial and temporal mechanisms for fast, energy-efficient differential-equation solving.

paragraphs: Symbolic regression seeks readable mathematical formulas that explain data. Equation Learner models can fit complex relationships, but increasing their size can activate unnecessary operators and make exact formula recovery unstable. This paper identifies a source of that problem: operators whose output is nonzero at zero can leave residual gradients on paths intended to remain inactive.

EQL-Z changes the operators to satisfy zero-point consistency, removing those residual gradients on silent paths. It also searches for structure gradually, expanding depth and width from a compact starting model. A validation score that penalizes complexity guides selection, after which BFGS fine-tuning refines the coefficients of the chosen expression.

These steps address both why redundant structure becomes active and how much structure the model is allowed to retain. Experiments on synthetic and real-world data report substantial improvements over vanilla EQL in exact equation recovery and generalization within and beyond the training distribution. Performance approaches leading symbolic regression baselines. The findings support combining training stability with explicit structural control when the goal is recovering a concise equation.
icml-2026-stabilizing-equation-learning-.tldr: EQL-Z combines zero-point-consistent operators and gradual structure search to recover simpler equations more reliably.

paragraphs: Customizing multimodal language models through fine-tuning services can expose them to poisoned training examples. This paper identifies attention allocation divergence as a shared backdoor fingerprint: poisoned samples disturb how attention is distributed among system instructions, visual inputs, and the user’s text. The authors describe this pattern as independent of the trigger’s particular form.

Tri-Component Attention Profiling, or TCAP, uses that observation to filter suspicious examples without supervised detection signals. It separates cross-modal attention maps into the three functional components, then applies Gaussian mixture profiling to identify attention heads responsive to triggers. An expectation-maximization-based voting process combines the resulting evidence to isolate poisoned samples.

The approach focuses on the model’s response to an example, allowing its detection signal to span different trigger appearances and modalities. Experiments across multiple multimodal model architectures and attack methods report consistently strong detection performance. These results support attention profiling as a practical unsupervised defense for fine-tuning data. The broad fingerprint claim is backed by the reported diversity of evaluations, rather than implying that every possible future attack has been tested.
icml-2026-tcap-tri-component-attention-p.tldr: TCAP detects poisoned multimodal fine-tuning samples by profiling shifts in attention across instructions, images, and user text.

paragraphs: Test-time training with key–value binding is often described as a sequence layer that learns to memorize mappings while processing an input. This paper identifies model behaviors that conflict with that explanation. It revisits the mathematical formulation and shows that a broad class of these architectures can instead be expressed as learned linear attention operators.

The reformulation supplies a common description for multiple test-time training variants. It explains previously puzzling behaviors while showing how their computation relates to a standard linear attention form with enhanced representational capacity. The scope is a broad class of architectures using this formulation, rather than a statement about every method that adapts during inference.

This interpretation also has practical consequences. It enables principled simplifications of model architecture and fully parallel formulations that preserve performance while improving efficiency. Reducing diverse variants to a common operator makes their computational structure easier to analyze and reorganize. The contribution therefore combines a revised account of what these layers compute with concrete opportunities to make that computation simpler and more efficient.
icml-2026-test-time-training-with-kv-bin.tldr: A broad class of key–value test-time training layers can be reformulated as learned linear attention, enabling simpler and more parallel computation.

paragraphs: Vision-language post-training commonly uses supervised examples to add knowledge or reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to improve performance. Each has a weakness in the paper’s account: supervised tuning can yield suboptimal performance, while reward-based tuning is constrained by existing model knowledge. Running them sequentially adds substantial computation and can lead to catastrophic forgetting.

ViSurf combines the two forms of learning in one stage. After analyzing their objectives, the authors construct a framework that injects ground-truth labels into reinforcement-learning rollouts. This lets external supervision and internal reinforcement operate together. Three additional reward-control strategies are introduced to support stable training and optimization.

Experiments report consistent improvements over supervised fine-tuning alone, reinforcement learning alone, and the conventional two-stage pipeline across diverse benchmarks. Further analysis supports the framework’s derivation and design. The central contribution is a way to connect learning from known answers with learning from rewards during the same training process, addressing the separation that can make sequential post-training expensive and prone to losing previously acquired knowledge.
icml-2026-visurf-visual-supervised-and-r.tldr: ViSurf combines ground-truth supervision and verifiable-reward reinforcement learning in a single vision-language post-training stage.

paragraphs: Emotional signals can occupy only a small part of a multimodal input, leaving them vulnerable to being overwhelmed by irrelevant context. This paper approaches emotion recognition as inference about a hidden emotional state from noisy observations. That perspective motivates controlling which tokens contribute to a prediction while leaving the model’s parameters frozen.

World-Model inspired Emotion-aware Token Refinement, or WETR, implements that control through two mechanisms. Noise-suppressed Token Selection reduces redundant information within each modality. State-strengthened Token Reweighting increases the influence of tokens relevant to the emotional decision. Together, they reshape how the existing model uses its input without requiring additional training.

Experiments on multiple emotion-recognition benchmarks report consistent improvements in accuracy and stability, alongside better token-level interpretability. The contribution goes beyond prompting the model to reason more carefully: it directly regulates token selection and weighting so sparse emotional evidence receives more useful attention. The findings support this as a practical way to improve frozen models when costly fine-tuning is undesirable and irrelevant context would otherwise dilute the evidence.
icml-2026-world-model-inspired-emotion-a.tldr: WETR improves emotion recognition without training by suppressing noisy tokens and strengthening emotionally relevant ones.
